archetype.name: Playoff Team (ball-control)
archetype.definition: A team that wins by holding the ball longer than anyone and getting off the field on third down, with an efficient Caleb Williams passing game on top and a turnover habit that keeps it out of the top tier.

report.headline: A real winner built on clock control and third-down stops, not just luck
report.take:
Last year's 11-win Bears were a mirage in some ways: the league's best turnover margin, 2.82 wins over expected and a defense ranked 21st in EPA. This version is sturdier. Net EPA ranks 8th, the point differential is 5.3 a game, and the defense has climbed to 15th in EPA allowed with a 6th-ranked success rate. The record is still a little ahead of the play, 1.12 wins over expected with the differential implying 3.9 wins, but this is no longer a team living on bounces. If anything, it has won while losing the turnover battle, at -0.7 a game, 26th in the league.

The identity under Ben Johnson in year two is possession. Chicago leads the league with 35.5 minutes of possession a game, sits 7th in offensive success rate and 3rd in yards per game, and its defense allows conversions on just 26.1% of third downs, best in the league. Long drives plus short opposing drives shrink the game and protect a defense that has real holes. The pass rush does the heavy lifting: a 27.8% pressure rate and an 8.4% sack rate, both 3rd.

The quarterback carousel is what the record hides. Williams started Weeks 1, 2, 6 and 7, Case Keenum won both of his starts on defense and field position, and Tyson Bagent's one start was the 31-7 collapse in Green Bay: five turnovers and -16.7 passing EPA, a single game that accounts for much of the ugly turnover margin. Since Williams came back the passing game has been strong, with 10.6 and 13.6 passing EPA against Atlanta and New England. The run game is the other quiet issue. The 291 rushing yards in Carolina flatter it; rushing EPA was negative in every game after Week 1, and it ranks 12th for the season.

The flaw that should worry people is big plays. The defense ranks 30th in explosive pass rate and dead last in EPA on deep throws. It has covered for that by winning on third down and harassing quarterbacks, a formula that holds against mediocre passers but breaks against good ones. The back half of the schedule has Detroit twice, Buffalo and Jacksonville, so the margin for that weakness gets thinner.

strengths.title: Owning the clock and third down
strengths.body: Chicago leads the league in time of possession and allows the lowest third-down conversion rate. The two feed each other: a 7th-ranked offensive success rate sustains drives, and a defense that gets off the field hands the ball right back. It is a repeatable style rather than a fluky one, though the third-down number is likely to drift toward average over a full season.

strengths.title: A top-three pass rush
strengths.body: The defense pressures on 27.8% of dropbacks and sacks on 8.4%, both 3rd in the league, and it posted five sacks in Atlanta. Pressure is the stickiest defensive trait and the main reason a secondary that gives up deep shots still ranks 6th in success rate allowed. Losing linebacker T.J. Edwards hurts the second level, not the rush itself.

strengths.title: Williams' passing game is humming
strengths.body: Passing EPA ranks 10th for the season despite three games from backups, and the Williams starts since his return were the two best passing days after the opener. Luther Burden III, Colston Loveland and Rome Odunze spread the targets, so the offense is not leaning on one receiver. With Cole Kmet on injured reserve, Loveland's role only grows.

concerns.title: The deep ball is wide open
concerns.body: No defense in the league allows more EPA on deep passes, and only two allow a higher rate of explosive completions. The rush and the third-down stops have hidden this against middling quarterbacks, but this is a real coverage flaw rather than a cost of the style, and the late-season slate is full of offenses that can punish it. A banged-up corner room, with Malik Muhammad II questionable, does not help.

concerns.title: Giveaways and flags
concerns.body: The turnover margin ranks 26th, and the five giveaways in Green Bay show how fast a backup quarterback can sink a game. With Williams back the ball security has steadied, but the line commits 3.9 penalties a game (26th) and Atlanta drew 133 penalty yards, which undercuts the drive-sustaining offense the team depends on.

concerns.title: Stalled against the one elite defense
concerns.body: The only top-tier defense Chicago has faced, Minnesota, now 1st in defensive EPA, held a Williams-led offense to three points, sacked him four times and pushed passing EPA negative. The protection ranks 19th in pressure rate allowed and 23rd in sacks allowed, and the run game has rarely made life easier. Seattle's defense profiles a lot like that one.

trend.note: Game-to-game quality has tracked the quarterback: an explosive opener and two strong recent Williams games, sandwiched around a defense-carried Keenum stretch and a five-turnover blowout with Bagent. With Williams healthy the arrow points up, but the sample of stable play is short.

nextGame.headline: Bears' pass rush meets Seattle's leakiest-in-league line, minus Charles Cross
nextGame.body:
This is the Bears' sternest test since the Minnesota loss. Seattle's defense ranks 2nd in EPA allowed and 3rd against both pass and run, and it allows the fewest explosive pass plays and the least EPA on deep throws in the league. Its offense is the opposite: 25th in EPA, 29th in rushing EPA and dead last in pressure rate allowed. The Book has Seattle by 3 with a 46.5 total, and Chicago is +142 on the moneyline after 11 days of rest following its Thursday game.

Availability tilts toward Chicago's strength. Seattle's left tackle Charles Cross, a 98%-snap starter, is doubtful with a high ankle sprain, which puts a weak protection unit against the league's 3rd-ranked pass rush. Drew Lock is out with an elbow injury, so Sam Darnold should start again, and the backfield is thin with Zach Charbonnet out and Jadarian Price only designated to return. Chicago is missing linebacker T.J. Edwards and back Kyle Monangai, has Cole Kmet on injured reserve, and may not have corner Malik Muhammad II.

waysToWin.title: Collapse the pocket on Darnold
waysToWin.body: Seattle allows pressure more often than any team and gets its quarterback hit at the 30th-ranked rate, and now it likely plays without Cross. Chicago's rush has been the defense's best unit all year. If it forces Seattle off schedule, a 25th-ranked offense with a 29th-ranked run game has little to fall back on.

waysToWin.title: Dink, drive and finish in the red zone
waysToWin.body: Seattle shuts down the deep ball but ranks only 21st in EPA allowed on short throws, which suits a Bears offense built on success rate and long possessions with Burden and Loveland underneath. The real opening comes inside the 20, where Seattle allows touchdowns at the 30th-ranked rate. Long drives that end in seven rather than three are how Chicago wins a low-possession game.

waysToWin.title: Win the field-position game on special teams
waysToWin.body: Both teams are among the league's best on special teams, and with two good defenses a punt-return swing or a long field goal can decide it. Chicago ranks 5th in special-teams EPA a game; neutralizing Seattle's unit keeps short fields away from a Seattle offense that struggles to drive the length of the field.

waysToLose.title: A repeat of the Minnesota game
waysToLose.body: Seattle's defense pressures at the 4th-ranked rate, hits quarterbacks at the 3rd-ranked rate and allows the 2nd-lowest success rate. Chicago's line has been middling in pass protection and its run game has posted negative EPA most weeks, so the offense could spend the night behind the sticks the way it did in a three-point loss to Minnesota.

waysToLose.title: One deep shot over the top
waysToLose.body: Chicago allows the most deep-pass EPA in the league, and a struggling offense needs only one or two explosive plays to steal a game like this. If Rashid Shaheed is cleared and a banged-up corner group, possibly without Muhammad, gets beaten deep, the pass rush's work is undone in one snap.

waysToLose.title: Losing the turnover battle
waysToLose.body: Both teams sit at -0.7 turnovers a game, but Seattle's defense has 10 takeaways, 7th in the league, and in a game projected to be tight a single giveaway on Chicago's side of the field may decide it. The Bears have offset turnovers with clock control against weaker defenses; that cushion shrinks against this one.

nextGame.watch: How often the Bears' rush beats Seattle's replacement left tackle: if Darnold is under pressure early, Chicago can play its clock-control game with a lead.

restOfSeason.body:
The core of this team should hold up: the pass rush, the possession-heavy offense and a Williams-led passing game that has been efficient whenever he has played. A turnover margin dragged down by one backup-quarterback disaster should improve with Williams healthy, which offsets some regression in the modest luck already baked into the record. What will not hold is the league-best third-down defense with a deep secondary this porous. Expect third-down conversions and points allowed to creep up, especially against Detroit, Buffalo and Jacksonville.

The schedule splits cleanly. Tampa Bay, New Orleans and Miami are winnable games, while two games with Detroit and trips to Buffalo and Minnesota decide the division and seeding. Minnesota's top-ranked defense already beat Chicago once, and the finale in Minneapolis may matter. A wild-card berth is the most likely outcome, with the division title realistic only if Williams stays upright and the deep coverage tightens.
swingFactors: Deep-pass coverage against Detroit, Buffalo and Jacksonville
